title: Acute Pancreatitis - 40-Year-Old Man with Upper Abdominal Pain
patient_instructions: You are Michael Turner, a 40-year-old man. You came in with severe upper abdominal (epigastric) pain that started this afternoon after a large lunch with several glasses of wine. The pain is constant, bores through to your back, and nothing you have tried has helped. You have discovered that leaning forward eases it a little, so you sit hunched forward in the chair - do NOT volunteer this, but if the candidate asks about position or notices how you are sitting, confirm that leaning forward helps and lying back makes it worse. You feel nauseated and have vomited once. Last night you drank alcohol heavily at a party. You take semaglutide (Ozempic) weekly for weight and blood sugar - only mention this if the candidate asks a proper medication question. If asked about weight: yes, you have lost 3 kg over the last month, and it was intentional (you have been dieting) - say this plainly if probed. Ideas: you think you have 'a bad stomach from the greasy food'. Concerns: you are frightened by how severe the pain is. Expectations: you want strong pain relief and to know what is wrong. Affect: visibly in pain, restless, grimacing, cooperative but distracted by discomfort. Do not use medical jargon; answer only what is asked.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in the Emergency Department of a rural NSW hospital. Michael Turner, a 40-year-old man, presents with severe upper abdominal pain that came on after lunch. Tasks: (1) Confirm haemodynamic stability, then take a focused, structured history for approximately 6 minutes, using a systematic pain assessment and screening for red flags and differentials of upper abdominal pain. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis with your reasons, and briefly outline relevant differentials, to the patient in plain language. You are not required to perform a physical examination.
examiner_instructions: Assess whether the candidate first checks haemodynamic stability, then explores the pain systematically (site, onset after large meal/alcohol, character, radiation to back, positional relief on leaning forward, severity), and takes a structured medication history that surfaces the GLP-1 agonist. Reward candidates who quantify the volunteered weight loss (3 kg, 1 month, intentional) and correctly judge it a pseudo red flag rather than anchoring on cancer, and who are not misled by the large meal into diagnosing a purely biliary cause. The expected diagnosis is acute pancreatitis (alcohol plus GLP-1 agonist). Prompt only if stuck: 'Is there anything about how the patient is sitting you want to explore?' Award communication marks for empathy and offering analgesia during the history.

criteria: Systematic pain assessment including onset, radiation to back and positional relief on leaning forward
Structured medication history eliciting GLP-1 agonist (semaglutide/Ozempic) and alcohol quantified in standard drinks
Quantifies the volunteered weight loss (amount, duration, intentional) rather than accepting it at face value
Identifies acute pancreatitis as the most likely diagnosis
Justifies with alcohol, GLP-1 agonist and classic positional/back-radiating epigastric pain
Does not anchor on gallbladder disease or cancer despite the distractors
Recognises this as a time-critical emergency requiring urgent bloods (serum lipase) and ED-level care
Offers appropriate analgesia and antiemetic; nil by mouth and IV fluids flagged
States GLP-1 agonist should be withheld and reviewed
Offers analgesia early rather than after completing the history

red_flags: Constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting - suspect acute pancreatitis requiring urgent lipase and ED assessment
Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension) signalling severe pancreatitis/SIRS - escalate immediately
Failure to quantify a volunteered symptom such as weight loss, risking either false alarm (cancer) or missed significance
Do not misattribute the presentation to biliary colic and discharge - untreated pancreatitis can deteriorate rapidly
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines, Gastrointestinal): acute pancreatitis - diagnose with serum lipase >3x upper limit of normal, keep nil by mouth, give aggressive IV crystalloid, analgesia and antiemetics, and assess severity early
RACGP / eTG: GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g. semaglutide) are a recognised cause of drug-induced pancreatitis and should be withheld and reviewed
Australian alcohol guidelines (NHMRC): no more than 10 standard drinks per week and no more than 4 on any one day - quantify intake in standard drinks
Call 000 / arrange urgent ED transfer for a suspected acute abdomen deteriorating in the community
learning_objectives: Apply a structured pain assessment to undifferentiated upper abdominal pain and use positional and dietary triggers to separate pancreatitis, biliary colic and peptic ulcer disease
Take a deliberate medication history and recognise GLP-1 agonists as a pancreatitis risk factor
Quantify every volunteered red flag before assigning significance, recognising the 2025-pattern pseudo red flag design
Outline Australian initial management of acute pancreatitis
key_points: Constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by sitting forward and worse supine, with nausea/vomiting is the classic pancreatitis descriptor
Serum lipase is preferred over amylase and is diagnostic at >3x the upper limit of normal
Intentional 3 kg loss over 1 month is not a significant red flag - always quantify how much, over how long, and whether intentional
Weigh multiple conflicting clues together rather than anchoring on a single finding

citations.claim: Time-critical acute abdominal presentations require rapid recognition and a safe diagnostic strategy, underpinning asking about haemodynamic stability first.
Acute severe abdominal pain has surgical-emergency differentials (peritonitis, obstruction, appendicitis) that must be excluded by structured questioning.
Australian management recommendations should be checked against the current Therapeutic Guidelines (tg.org.au) as the reference standard.
